items.prose: After `git fetch`, your `main` has A to D, then F and G. `origin/main` has A to D, then E1, E2 and E3.
items.question: What does `git status` say?

options.text: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 2 and 3 different commits each
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits
options.why: That ignores E1 to E3. Origin has commits you lack too.

options.text: Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 3 commits
options.why: That ignores F and G, which only you have.

options.text: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 6 and 7 different commits each
options.why: You counted whole histories. Only commits after the shared D differ.

feedback.correct: Two of yours, three of theirs, after the shared commit D.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only the commits after the last shared one.

explain.text: Both histories share A to D. After that you have F and G, and origin has E1, E2 and E3. Status reports 2 and 3, and a pull will merge them.

items.prose:
`trades.csv` has a header line `date,ticker,side,qty`, then six trades in AAPL, MSFT, AAPL, NVDA, MSFT, AAPL.

```sh
$ cut -d, -f2 trades.csv | sort | uniq | wc -l
```
items.question: What number does it print?

widget.label: Number printed
widget.accept: 4: AAPL, MSFT, NVDA and the header word ticker.

feedback.correct: Four distinct lines, the header word included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow all seven lines through the pipeline.

byKey.three: You counted the tickers only. The header word `ticker` is a distinct line too.
byKey.seven: You counted every line. uniq collapses the repeats after sort.
byKey.six: You counted the trades. After sort, uniq keeps one line per distinct value.

explain.text: cut sends seven lines, header included. sort and uniq leave AAPL, MSFT, NVDA and ticker. wc -l counts 4; add `tail -n +2` after cut to drop the header.

items.prose: Write `run_all.sh`. It should give `results.csv` one header and one row per ticker for SPY, QQQ, IWM, EFA and TLT, however often it runs.
items.question: Put the lines of the script in order.

lines.text: `for T in SPY QQQ IWM EFA TLT; do`

feedback.correct: Clear and write the header once, then append inside the loop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The file must be cleared before the loop, not in it.

byKey.header: The header line clears the file, so it must come before the loop. Inside, it would wipe each row.
byKey.body: The body sits between `for ... do` and `done`.
byKey.shebang: `#!/bin/bash` must be the very first line.
byKey.for: The loop opens after the header and before the body.
byKey.done: `done` closes the loop, so it comes last.

explain.text: The `#!` line names the shell and must be first. One `>` before the loop clears the file and writes the header. Inside the loop `>>` appends, so five rows follow.

items.prose: A project's `.gitignore` holds three lines: `*.csv`, `results/` and `.env`. Nothing was committed before it was written.
items.question: Which files will a fresh clone be missing? Select all that apply.

options.why: `.env` matches the exact name only. `.env.example` is committed.
No pattern matches a .py file at the top level.

feedback.correct: Every file a pattern matches, wherever it sits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each file against all three patterns.

byKey.fix: `*.csv` matches in every folder, the test's small file included. The test will fail on the clone.

explain.text: `*.csv` catches both CSV files, the test data included. `results/` catches everything in that folder, even a README. `.env` matches only that exact name, so `.env.example` survives.

items.prose: Git's `ahead` and `behind` counts compare two histories. For two straight histories, oldest commit first, the shared commits are the run at the start where both lists agree. Everything after that run differs.
items.question: Write `ahead_behind(local, remote)`. It returns a tuple: commits only in local, then commits only in remote.

widget.label: ahead_behind.py
widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. Each result must equal the expected tuple exactly. Lists may be empty, and may differ from the very first commit.

feedback.correct: Count the shared start, then subtract it from each length.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test: which lists did it use?

explain.text: Walk both lists together while they agree; that count is the shared history. Local is ahead by the rest of its length, and behind by the rest of remote's. In ['A','B','X','Y'] against ['A','B','C'], 2 are shared, so the answer is (2, 1).

items.prose: `load_dotenv()` reads `.env` files. Write a small version. Skip blank lines and lines starting with `#`. Allow an `export ` prefix. Split at the first `=`, and strip spaces round the name and value. Remove one pair of matching quotes round the value. Skip lines with no `=`. A later line wins.
items.question: Write `parse_env(text)`, returning a dictionary of names to values.

widget.label: parse_env.py
widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Each dictionary must equal the expected one exactly. Values may contain `=` and spaces.

feedback.correct: Every rule handled, in the right order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test's input line by line.

explain.text: `partition('=')` splits at the first `=` only, so URLs with `=` survive. The `export ` prefix comes off before the split. Quotes are removed only when the first and last characters match.

items.title: A key in a public repository
items.prompt:
Your Stage 1 repository is public. Three days ago you pushed a commit that put your live data API key, `pk_live_...`, in `download.py`. Yesterday a second commit deleted that line.

Write the plan you would follow now, in order. For each step, say what you do, the commands where they apply, and why. Explain why the second commit did not fix the problem, and say what rewriting the history would and would not achieve.
items.model:
**1. Revoke the key first.** Log in to the data provider, revoke `pk_live_...` and issue a new key. It sat in a public repository for three days. Bots scan GitHub for keys within minutes, so assume it was copied. Nothing done in Git can recall a copy someone already has.

**2. See how far it spread.** Search the whole history for the key and any other secret:

```sh
$ git log -p -S "pk_live" --all
```

`-S` lists every commit that added or removed that text. Check the provider's usage log for calls you did not make.

**3. Take the key out of the code.** Make `download.py` read it from the environment:

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
key = os.environ["POLYGON_API_KEY"]
```

Put the new key in `.env`, add `.env` to `.gitignore`, and check with `git check-ignore -v .env`. Commit a `.env.example` holding `POLYGON_API_KEY=` with no value.

**4. Clean the history if you wish.** A new commit that deletes the line leaves the old commit intact. Removing it means rewriting history with a tool such as `git filter-repo`, then force-pushing. That changes every commit hash after the leak, so every collaborator must re-clone or reset. It tidies the repository; it does not un-leak the key, which is why step 1 comes first.

**5. Tell the team, and prevent a repeat.** Say what leaked, when, and that the key is revoked. Turn on GitHub's secret scanning and push protection, so a key in a format GitHub recognises is blocked before it reaches GitHub.

**Why not just delete the line?** Because commit C is a snapshot. `git show C:download.py` still prints the key, in every clone made in those three days.

rubric.text: Revokes or rotates the key first, and says why: copies already made cannot be recalled
Explains that a commit deleting the line leaves the key in the earlier commit, readable with git show or git log -p
Moves the key to an environment variable or .env read by the code, with .env in .gitignore, checked with git check-ignore
Treats history rewriting (git filter-repo plus a force push) as optional clean-up, with its cost to collaborators
Searches the history for other leaks or checks the provider's usage log
Tells the team, or turns on secret scanning or push protection

items.prose: Sam merged your `mdd` request with **Squash and merge**: D, E and F became one new commit, S, on `main`. Still on `mdd`, you run `git switch -c costs`, commit K and open a new request. It shows D, E, F and K.
items.question: What went wrong, and what fixes it?

options.text: `costs` grew from the old `mdd`. Switch to main, pull, then make the branch
A GitHub fault: D, E and F will vanish when K is merged
options.why: GitHub is right. main holds S, a different commit, so D, E and F really are missing from it.
mdd is merged already. Pushing it again changes nothing about where `costs` started.
Pulling `costs` fetches its own branch. The problem is the commit `costs` started from.

feedback.correct: A new branch starts from wherever you stand.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which commit `costs` grew from, and whether main contains it.

explain.text: You branched from F, so `costs` carries D, E and F under K. After a squash, main holds S instead, a different commit, so all four look new. Start each change from an up-to-date main: `git switch main`, `git pull`, `git switch -c costs`.

items.title: A .gitignore for an options project
items.prose:
You are about to push an options-pricing project to GitHub. Write its `.gitignore` from scratch.

**Commit** these, which you wrote by hand:

- `README.md`, `requirements.txt` and `.gitignore`
- `.env.example`, which names the keys with no values
- `src/pricer.py`, and `src/figures.py`, which draws the charts
- `notebooks/smile.ipynb` and `tests/test_pricer.py`
- `tests/fixtures/chain_small.parquet`, the 12 rows the tests read
- `data/README.md`, which says how to fetch the data
- `docs/figures/smile.png`, the one chart the README shows

**Keep out** these:

- everything else under `data/`, such as `data/raw/chains_2025.parquet` (2 GB, downloaded nightly) and `data/clean/chains_2025.parquet`
- every chart in the top-level `figures/` folder, which each run redraws
- the virtual environment, `.venv/`
- both keys: `.env` (live) and `.env.local` (paper trading)
- every `__pycache__/` and `.ipynb_checkpoints/` folder, in any folder

The rules must also hold for files added later in those places, not only for today's files. Two more rules of the file. A line starting with `!` takes back an earlier line for the paths it matches. A leading `/` ties a pattern to the project's top folder.

`ignored(path)` is loaded for you. It answers as `git check-ignore` would for your `GITIGNORE`, so use it to check your file.
items.question: Write the file in the string `GITIGNORE`, one pattern per line.

widget.label: gitignore.py
widget.solution:
GITIGNORE = """
# downloads; keep the note on fetching
data/*
!data/README.md
# charts each run redraws, top level only
/figures/
# rebuilt by Python and Jupyter, anywhere
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
# the virtual environment
.venv/
# keys
.env
.env.local
"""
widget.how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests through `ignored(path)`, which follows Git's own rules for one top-level `.gitignore`. Some tests use paths that are not in the lists above but fall under their rules.

feedback.correct: Every listed file lands on the right side, and so does every file added later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run `ignored` on the path in the first failing test and find the line that decides it.

byKey.test-3: Test 3: `data/README.md` is ignored. Once a folder itself is ignored, Git never looks inside it, so a `!` line cannot bring a file back. Ignore the folder's contents with `data/*` instead.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 adds new files under `data/`, one in a new subfolder. List the folder's contents with a pattern, not today's file names.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: the test fixture is ignored. A pattern on the file type, such as `*.parquet`, also catches the 12 rows the tests need.
byKey.test-7: Test 7: `docs/figures/smile.png` is ignored. A pattern whose only `/` is at the end matches at any depth, so it catches `docs/figures/` too. Tie it to the top folder.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has `__pycache__/` folders in other places. Name the folder alone, so the pattern matches it in any folder.
byKey.test-13: Test 13: `.env.example` is ignored. A pattern with a star, such as `.env*`, catches the template too. Name the two keys, or take the template back with `!`.

explain.text: `data/*` ignores what is inside `data/`, not the folder, so `!data/README.md` can take the note back. With `data/`, Git skips the whole folder. A pattern whose only `/` is at the end matches at any depth: right for `__pycache__/`, wrong for `figures/`.
